content: The introduction of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2006 marked a significant shift in the global recognition of mobility aids, assistive devices, and technologies as fundamental human rights. This was followed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2008, which developed comprehensive guidelines for the provision of manual wheelchairs in resource-limited settings. These guidelines were created through a consensus-driven process and provided detailed recommendations on wheelchair products, services, training, and policy. They also introduced the first definition of an appropriate wheelchair, which remains a cornerstone in current guidelines. The 2008 guidelines outlined eight essential service steps to ensure safe access to appropriate wheelchairs. To further support these efforts, WHO developed open-source Wheelchair Service Training Packages (WSTPs) to train individuals involved in the provision of manual wheelchairs. In 2015, the International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP) was established to enhance global wheelchair service delivery, including training and policy development. The ISWP also introduced a basic knowledge test, which has been taken by over 6,000 wheelchair service providers in its first five years, offering a pathway for competency assessment and certification. Resources like the WSTPs have been instrumental in helping countries build national wheelchair provision capacity. Despite progress in the wheelchair sector, there remains a pressing need for global policies and standards for wheelchair provision. In 2018, a Wheelchair Stakeholders’ Meeting in Bangalore, India, identified the establishment of global service standards as a top priority. That same year, the 71st World Health Assembly endorsed the first resolution on assistive technology, urging the development of policies and minimum standards for priority assistive products and services to ensure safety, quality, cost-effectiveness, and appropriateness. WHO's new guidelines aim to assist Member States in achieving these goals, with a focus on wheelchairs while also informing the broader assistive technology sector. The current guidelines consolidate the eight service steps from the 2008 guidelines into four key service delivery steps, ensuring greater relevance across all settings and reflecting the sector's evolution. These guidelines align with other WHO documents, such as the Global Report on Assistive Technology, the World Report on Disability, and the WHO Global Report on Health Equity for Persons with Disabilities. They also complement WHO standards for prosthetics and orthotics, community-based rehabilitation guidelines, and the framework for action on strengthening health systems. An appropriate wheelchair, as defined by WHO, must meet the user’s needs and environmental conditions, provide proper fit and postural support, be safe and durable, be available in the country, and be affordable to obtain, maintain, and service. Such wheelchairs enable mobility, improve health and functionality, and serve as a means to exercise human rights. They are essential for inclusion and participation, benefiting individuals, families, and society. Conversely, inappropriate wheelchairs can lead to poor health outcomes, secondary complications, participation barriers, and disruptions in use, ultimately undermining the user’s ability to exercise their rights. Wheelchair users are a diverse group with varying needs, goals, and life roles. They may include individuals of any age, gender, or socioeconomic status, living in rural, peri-urban, or urban environments. Some may use wheelchairs all day, every day, while others may use them only when their walking capacity is exceeded. Certain groups, such as children, older persons, people with disabilities, and those with chronic health conditions, require special consideration to ensure their mobility needs are met equitably. Children need timely access to wheelchairs to support their physical, cognitive, and social development. Regular adjustments and access to wheelchair services are crucial to accommodate their growth and changing needs. Older persons, who represent the largest age group in need of wheelchairs, benefit from appropriate wheelchairs that help maintain independence and dignity while mitigating health impacts associated with aging. People with disabilities often require wheelchairs tailored to their specific conditions, such as cerebral palsy, spinal cord injuries, or neurodegenerative diseases. Similarly, individuals with chronic health conditions, such as stroke or diabetes, benefit from timely wheelchair provision to improve health outcomes and quality of life. In summary, the provision of appropriate wheelchairs is a critical component of health and social systems, enabling mobility, inclusion, and participation for diverse populations. The WHO guidelines provide a comprehensive framework to ensure safe and effective wheelchair use, addressing the needs of individuals and supporting global efforts to improve access to assistive technologies.
